newsitem.title: UK: Number of UK equity market players to fall -survey.
newsitem.headline: Number of UK equity market players to fall -survey.

text.p: Britain's equity markets may be booming but consolidation of the industry continues apace, according to a survey published on Tuesday.

The 1997 Reuters survey of British larger company investment research, sales and trading said the relatively small numbers of fund managers, analysts and salespeople receiving support in the poll highlighted the growing concentration in the industry.
NatWest Securities held on to top spot in the annual weighted survey of fund managers, compiled by Tempest Consultants, but its lead slipped after a year which saw considerable turnover of staff.

Finance directors opted for Swiss bank UBS as the best broker while NatWest's oil team, led by Fergus MacLeod, was again voted best sector team. SBC Warburg won both best broker execution and best broker sales.
Finance directors voted Mercury Asset Management as best fund management group and the team at Schroder Investment Management as best individual fund manager, instead of choosing a single individual.
Pressure for consolidation was blamed on expansion plans at securities and fund management groups as well as higher market levels and strong revenues and profits.
"Viewed from all three corners of the equity triangle, growing concentration through corporate activity is the natural consequence of the relentless pressure," it said.

The largest companies were becoming more dominant due to globalisation, deregulation and a drive for shareholder value. This in turn is leading to further growth of sector coverage by "buy" and "sell" side research departments.
It was also resulting in the exploitation of global investment banking opportunities by the most focused and integrated firms.

An increasing concentration of British equity funds resulted from competition and an increased focus on costs and performance as well as outsourcing of in-house company pension funds and mergers and acquisitions arising from bank and insurance company competition.

These factors are leading to a migration of funds to the best performers and have already resulted in the absorption of eight significant fund management groups during 1996/97, with more in the pipeline.
They have also led to larger funds being managed by fewer managers, the survey said.

The survey also said there are too many analysts following too many companies, too many brokers selling to fewer fund management groups and merger activity resulted from competition and a need for more capital adequacy.

This increasing concentration of brokers' analysts meant the securities industry was shouldering high costs, there was increasing discrimination between winners and losers and a shakeout is on the cards when the market turns.
Other themes highlighted included a strong increase in demand for on-line research.

It also found serious gaps were developing between what fund managers wanted and what they actually got and this was leading fund management groups to use fewer brokers and increase their own in-house research.
Fund management groups were making greater use of in-house crossed dealing and programme trading and the proportion of British equity trading which bears commission has dropped, the survey found.

And while dealers at fund management groups are warming to the prospect of an order driven system -- where shares are bought automatically and sold via computer instead of being dealt by a traditional market maker -- they still think liquidity and speed of execution will suffer.
But this was played down by the London Stock Exchange which said there was evidence to show order-driven share trading would offer benefits to large and small investors
Another theme to have emerged from the survey is that finance directors of the quoted companies were increasing their direct contact with fund managers.
The survey found they prefer one-to-one meetings with fund managers and brokers' analysts rather than group meetings, identifying with individuals rather than teams.
But it also found fund managers have markedly different ideas about how analysts should be spending their time compared with how analysts are actually allocating their efforts.

While fund managers said they would like 46 percent of analysts' time to be spent on fundamental research in future, the analysts themselves said they intend spending only 36 percent of their time on this aspect.
